title: Learning About Algorithm Auditing in Five Steps: Scaffolding How High School Youth Can Systematically and Critically Evaluate Machine Learning Applications
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to support high school students in critically evaluating machine learning systems through algorithm auditing. The authors argue that while AI education often introduces students to AI/ML concepts, there is little guidance on how to help them systematically investigate how such systems work, what biases they may contain, and what their broader implications are. To fill this gap, the paper proposes a five-step auditing process for learning activities: developing a hypothesis, generating systematic inputs, running tests, analyzing results, and reporting findings.

The approach is presented through a case study from a two-week summer workshop in an after-school science program in the northeastern United States. Fourteen rising high school sophomores worked in pairs to design and audit peer-created generative AI TikTok filters using TikTok Effect House. The workshop included scaffolds such as hypothesis examples, a two-axis input organizer, input-output tables, and guidance for reporting findings to peers. The paper focuses on one pair of students, Ishmael and Ziyi, to show how they engaged with each step of the audit process.

The main conclusion is that high school youth can meaningfully engage in a structured auditing workflow when given appropriate scaffolds and time. The authors found that the five-step model helped students move beyond ad hoc observations toward more systematic critique of AI behavior, including noticing gendered and racialized effects in a filter’s outputs. They also conclude that learner-centered scaffolding should blend expert auditing structure with youth-relevant, user-driven observations. The paper emphasizes that future classroom implementations will need further support for input generation, analysis, reporting, and teacher facilitation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative design-based case study with rich artifact and video analysis, but no comparison group, randomization, or quantitative estimate of learning impact. The methodology is credible for exploratory insight, yet it does not meet stronger causal-evidence criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a promising instructional approach for supporting critical AI evaluation, but it provides no measurable effect size and only a small workshop case study. Its impact is therefore informative but still unclear at the population level.

interventions.use_case: Scaffolded algorithm-auditing learning activity for high school students using peer-designed generative AI TikTok filters in TikTok Effect House, with five steps (hypothesis, input generation, testing, analysis, reporting) to evaluate model behavior and bias.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the five-step algorithm-auditing scaffold enabled 14 high school students to engage in systematic, critical evaluation of machine learning applications. In the focal case study, two students (Ishmael and Ziyi) were able to generate a hypothesis, build a 33-image test set, analyze outputs, and report findings about gendered and racialized filter behavior.
finding.measure: Qualitative case study of youth engagement with auditing steps; artifact analysis, screen/video recordings, and audit report content
finding.study_size: n=14 overall workshop; focal case study n=2
